Nurul Huq with S. M. Jahangir Alam, Mozammel Huq & Mrs. Rabiya Bhuiyan ----- For the petitioner.
Dinesh Chandra Chakraborty ----- For the opp. No.1.
parties:
Manjelat Ara Ahmed ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Sakhina Begum & ors ----- Opp. Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an order rejecting the prayer for release of property from attachment. The facts leading to this application, briefly stated are as follows: - One Kazi A. Latif, opposite party No, 2, entered into an agreement initially to transfer '055 acres of land of 3305 and 3306 with the petitioner on 9. 3. 69 for a sum of Taka 1000/- out of which, Taka 201/- was paid as earnest money. The petitioner subsequently came to learn that the aforesaid two plots of land felI in the saham of one Anjuman Ara Begum, a co-sharer of Kazi Abdul Latif, in the Partition Suit No. 274 of 1967, and Kazi Abdul Latif has got '121 acres from plot No. 3310. As Kazi A. Latif was avoiding to fulfill his part of the agreement by executing and registering a deed of sale in favour of the petitioner as agreed upon on 9.3.69 and as the plots in agreement therein fell into the saham of Anjuman Ara Begum, the petitioner was compelled to file Title Suit No. 247 of 1969 against him claiming '055 acres of land from the plot No. 3310 which fell into Kazi A. Latif's share, It has been alleged further by the petitioner that this suit was compromised between them on 24.6.71 on the term that if a sum of Taka 800/- is paid to the petitioner within December, 1971, the petitioner shall have no claim against him but in case of failure on the part of the opposite party No. 2 to pay the said amount within the stipulated time the petitioner will have the right to get the deed of sale executed and registered in her favour through Court. According to this term 2f compromise this suit was decreed on 24.6.71, but Kazi A. Latif having failed to return the money as stipulated, the petitioner filed Title Execution Case No. 9 of 1972 for having the deed executed and registered through the court and ultimately he got it executed and registered through the court on 19.6.72. 

 2. In the meantime it appears. that the opposite party No. 1 Sakhina Begum, brought a Title Suit No. 9 of 1972 against the opposite party No. 2, Kazi A. Latif, claiming title in certain land other than, the present suit land which was ultimately by an amendment converted into a suit for realisation of sum of Taka 8192/-. She also prayed for attachment before the judgment of '125 acres out of disputed plot No. 3310 purported to be belonging to opposite party No. 2. The petitioner on getting information about it  filed an application on the same date, i.e. 26.5.72 on which date the application for attachment was filed, objecting to the attachment before judgment. On that date the learned Judge on hearing the learned Advocate for the opposite party issued show cause notice upon the defendant opposite party No. 2 but meanwhile ordered attachment of the suit land before the judgment. He also noted in his order the fact of filing of the petition by the petitioner against the attachment and ordered that this objection be heard at the time of the hearing of suit. It appears that no such hearing of the objection petition did take place and the matter remained un-disposed. This Title Suit No. 9 of 1972 against the opposite party No. 2 was ultimately decreed on 22.6.73 for a sum of Taka 7500/- and opposite party No.1 filed Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1973 on 10.9.73 for realisation of the decreetal dues and prayed for sale of the attached '125 acres of land of plot No. 3310 which was advertised for sale in local Weekly and Daily. Thereafter the petitioner filed an application under Order 38, Rule 9 and 10 read with Order 21, Rule 58 of the Civil Procedure Code, which was registered as Misc. Case No. 37 of 1974, objecting to the attachment of '055 acres of land asserting again her title and possession, out of '125 acres of land, on the strength of decree dated 24.6.71 obtained in Title Suit No. 247 of 1969 and resulting in execution and registration of Kabala through Court on 19.6.72. 

 3. This application was registered by the opposite party No. 1, the decree holder, by filing a written objection alleging that the suit for Specific Performance of Contract of the land of plot No. 3310 was fraudulent and collusive and that the petitioner was never in possession of .055 acres of land of plot No. 3310 and have no interest or possession and as such this land cannot be released from attachment. 

 5. It may be mentioned at the outset that the opposite party No. 2 the judgment debtor was not entered appearance. It also does not appear that the office has got the return of services of notice upon him. The opposite party No. 1, the decree holder, who only contested before the executing Court, has appeared and filed an affidavit in opposition. The learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the Pettitioner. as well as for the opposite party have pressed for early hearing of this matter, and as the opposite party No. 2 being the judgment debtor and having not put any objection in this easel I think he is not a necessary party and, as such, this application can be heard in his absence. 

 6. Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the petitioner has strenuously urged that the learned Judge acted illegally in the exercise of his jurisdiction by refusing to release the property from the attachment. According to him, the learned Judge has overlooked the provision of Order 38, Rule 10 of the C. P. C. He has further submitted that the right and interest of the petitioner in the property having accrued prior to the purported attachment no claim for attachment IS enforceable against him. He has further contended that the Possession of the judgment debtor cannot be deemed to be on his own account but should be treated on account of the petitioner and as such the petitioner was entitled to have the land released from attachment. The learned Advocate, in this connection, has referred to the rulings reported in A.I.R. 1914. P.C. 129 in the case of Ragunath Dass and others Vs. Sundar Das Khetri and another where it has been held by their lordship of the Privy Council that attachment prevents and avoids any private alienation, but does not invalidate an alienation by operation of law such as is effected by a vesting order under the Insolvent Debtors Act of 1848, and an order for sale though it binds the parties does not confer title. He has also referred to I.L.R. 4 Allahabad 219 in the case of QurbanAli  Vs. Ashraf Ali. In this case a Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court held that a conveyance executed for the land in question under the decree made in pursuance of an award in favour of plaintiff which although was previously attached in execution of the decree of another case was nor a private alienation in the sense of section 276 of Act X of 1877 (now section 64) of the C.P.C. and the sale was, therefore, not void, under that section as against a claim enforceable under such attachment. The learned Advocate has cited the aforesaid two cases to show that in the present case even if the transfer  be held to be after attachment it was not a private transfer within the meaning of section 64 of the C. P. C. It may be convenient in this context to quote the section 64 of the C.P.C. 

 7. Transfer in the present case, according to the learned Advocate was not a voluntary transfer and cannot be deemed to be a private transfer inasmuch as it was in execution of a decree obtained by the petitioner in his suit for specific performance of Contract against the opposite party No.2. In this connection, he has cited, P.L.D. 1962 (S.C.) 119 same case 14 D.L.R. 113, Mohiuddin Molla Vs. The Province of East Pakistan and others, where their lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan considered the question as to the effect of the agreement for sale antecedent to the judgment and after considering the relevant statutory provisions applicable to the situation like this, namely, section 40 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, section 27 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and section 91 of the Trust Act, 1882, held that according to section 40 of the Transfer of Property Act an obligation annexed to the ownership of the property binds the transferee with notice and that an agreement for sale is an Obligation annexed to the ownership of the property is apparent and is in any case clear from illustration to section 40, and ultimately held that such an enticedent agreement for sale binds the purchaser at a Court sale. 

 8. The learned Advocate has also referred to A.I. R. 1943 Bombay 145 in the case of Yesh-vant Shankar Dunakhe Vs, Pyaraji Nurji Tamboli where it has been held that the principle laid down in order 38, rule 10 is not limited to attachment before the judgment. It applies to all attachment whether before the judgment or in course of execution. Where the purchase in pursuance of a decree for specific performance is subsequent to the attachment but the agreement in pursuance of which the decree has been passed was prior to the attachment the purchase prevails against the attachment. 

 9. Mr. Dinesh Chakraborty, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the decree holder opposite party No.1, has contended on the other hand that where an application under Order 21, rule 58 C. P. C., has been rejected and the Court has denied to release the property from attachment the only course left open to the claimant or objector is by a suit under order 21, rule 63, C. P. C. Further he has submitted that the relevant question in such case is the question of possession and if possession is not with the claimant but is found to be with the judgment debtor it must be shown that the judgment debtor was possessing not on his own account but on account of the claimant. Further he submits that in this case even if it be admitted that the claimant has got title perfected by executing a registered deed of sale 'through court, yet the judgment-debtor cannot be said to possess the attached property on account of or on behalf of the claimant. He will be deemed to possess on his own account and adversely against the claimant. In this connect ion the learned Advocate has cited I.L.R. 15 Allahabad 405, J. J. Guise Vs. Jairsraj & another, A.I.R. 1933 Nagpur 297 Jagannath and another Vs. Ganpatrao, 1 C.W.N. 617, Mohunt Bhagwan Ramanuj Das Vs. Khetter Moni Dassi, 64 C.L.J. 399, BattaKristo Paul and Co. Ltd. Vs. Harcndra Nath Ghose, A.I.R. 1939 Allahabad 117, Bachu Lal Vs. Ram Din; A.I.R. 1931, Lahore 666 Imemdin Vs. Mathra Das; LL.R. 14 Cal 617, Hamid Bakhut Mazumder Vs. Bukhtear Chand Matho; 16 D.L.R. rs.c.i 287 Mir Laik Ali Vs. Standard Vacuum Oil Company (Esso) and Abdur Razzak; and 11 I.L.R. (Cal) 229, Anand Coomari Vs. Ali Jamin. 

 11. In A.I.R. 1933 Nagpur 297 in the Case of  Jagannath and another Vs. Ganpat Rao, in a revisional application, it was found that objector's contention was that they have purchased the property one month before the attachment and claimed to have been in possession which the decree holder denied and pleaded that it was a bogus and fraudulent sale. The Court also found that the objectors though have purchased were not in possession. It was held: 

 14. The Court found that the houses had been sold to the objector by the judgment debtor, but that the sale had taken place after the institution of the suit in which the decree was passed. The learned Judge, therefore, held that the sale was made to defraud the decree bolder. It was held:- 

 15. In J.L.R.14 CaI. 617(DB)in a Revisional application the objector was found to be in possession but the Trial Court in coming to a finding whether his possession was on behalf of judgment debtor, enquired into the nature of his title as Mutwalli under Wakfnama which he found to be invalid and so much of the property attached as was dealt with by that wakfnama was liable to be sold in execution of the decree. In this context it was held:- 

 18.In the present case there is no dispute that, there was transfer in favour of the petitioner who is a third party. Whether that transfer is fraudulent or collusive, as raised by the decree holder, the onus to prove that is upon him. His present title is not a matter which requires to be decided in this case and cannot preclude the Court in doming to the finding whether or not an attachment should be allowed to continue in my opinion no question of title is involved in this case nor any question of adjudicating on the conflicting rights of the parties as to the title of the attached land. The facts are patent. The right of the claimant petitioner has accrued before attachment if not from the date of alleged agreement for sale on 9-3-1969 at least from the date of decree in Title Suit No. 247 of 1967 for specific performance of contract, namely, 24 6-71, long before the date of attachment before judgment on 26-5-72. Further the decree for specific performance of contract of sale has been effected by the execution of a registered deed of sale through Court on 19-6-70 only a few days after the date of attachment on 26-5-72 and, as such, it cannot also be said to be a private transfer within the meaning of section 64, C.P.C. and, therefore, it is valid against all claims enforceable under attachment. These facts cannot be ignored and the validity of attachment will have to be decided keeping these in view.
